title: why companies want throw switch electrification  ecmii 2026 06 15
text:
June 15 - Something happens when a system gets pushed too far. It fractures, reorders and comes back in a different shape. The global energy economy is at that point now. No single decision by any leader brought it here. The accumulated weight of interconnected pressures – geopolitical, economic, technological, logistical – has made the old order untenable, and the cracks are showing everywhere at once.
Two energy shocks in four years – conflict in the Middle East, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – and the cascading impacts of climate change are all symptoms of a global system built on fossil fuels and the machinery, combustion engines and industrial processes that burn them.
Last week at the Bonn climate change conference, the COP31 presidency called for a global effort to “electrify daily life”, and proposed a goal of meeting 35% of final energy demand with electricity by 2035.
Our latest annual poll, of nearly 2,000 senior executives, indicates that the business community appears to be moving in the same direction.
The research, in partnership with E3G and Global Renewables Alliance, examined business attitudes to electrification across 18 countries, exploring perceptions of energy security, competitiveness, investment barriers, policy support and business timelines for electrification.
Seventy-nine percent say geopolitical instability has made their own shift to electrification more urgent. Ninety-one percent say it will improve their energy security. And when asked for a timeline to electrify their operations, 90% say they expect to have largely electrified by 2035, with the vast majority wanting their country’s electricity to come from mainly renewable sources.
These are not ideological answers, they are the calculations of people watching energy costs eat into revenue. Data from the International Energy Agency shows that investment in electricity supply and infrastructure is projected to reach nearly $1.6 trillion in 2026 – close to $2 trillion when end-use electrification is included. Grid spending alone is approaching $550 billion, up nearly 20% year-on-year.
Despite the polling taking in extremely diverse markets, the findings are remarkably consistent. In the United States, where the political environment is increasingly hostile to clean energy, 91% of business leaders say electrification would make their business more competitive – the highest figure among advanced economies.
In China, 92% expect to electrify operations by 2035, with electrification seen as a competitiveness strategy. In Turkey and Australia, the two nations co-hosting this year’s COP31 climate summit, 93% of Turkish executives expect to electrify by 2035. In Australia, 65% say they would consider moving operations overseas if their government failed to support them to electrify.
In most emerging markets, the energy crisis has hit businesses and homes more directly, leading to rationing and emergency measures.
The polling reflects this, showing that in Indonesia 99% of business leaders expect to electrify by 2035 or earlier, the Philippines stands at 97% and India at 96%. All three figures are higher than every advanced economy surveyed.
Recent analysis from Ember backs up the findings that electrification is becoming a strategic response to energy insecurity in Asia, helping countries reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels while strengthening competitiveness and resilience.
In Europe, French President Emmanuel Macron recently convened industry and financiers around a national plan to increase the share of electricity in France’s final energy consumption. And polling across European countries shows the vast majority of businesses in France, the UK, Germany and Poland expect to electrify within the decade. Support for grid investment is overwhelming across all four markets, hitting 90% in the UK, 88% across France, with Poland at 88% and Germany 87%.
But frustration at the pace of change is the other half of this story. Sixty-nine percent say they are electrifying their own operations faster than governments are preparing the system. The constraints cited include insufficient government incentives, inadequate grid investment and policy instability between electoral cycles. Half have already delayed or cancelled electrification projects because of these barriers.
What businesses want is not complicated: grids that can handle the load, grants and incentives that make the upfront cost of switching bearable, planning systems that move at the speed of investment decisions and long-term policy frameworks that survive changes of government. None of these is beyond reach. The problem is not that the solutions are unclear, it is that they need to arrive together, and they need to arrive at speed.
As G7 leaders meet in Evian, France, this week, global energy security, including the push for energy independence and electrification, needs to be high on their agenda.
Businesses are saying they are ready to throw the switch on electrification because the old fossil fuel system no longer benefits them or the wider economy and communities where they operate. It’s time for governments to catch up.
